The members of this family who study Prajñā have all exerted their strength to provide external protection.
Were it not for the fact that we possess great karmic conditions from former lives, how could this be so? Nevertheless, when gathering with others, one’s body and mind must be authentic.

If the mind is authentic, then in every movement and action, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, and in every word or silence, there will be nothing that is not authentic. How could this be otherwise?
One does not see the Way of the ancients: "This very mind, mind, mind is Buddha; the most wondrous thing in the worlds of the ten directions.
Its transverse and vertical wondrous functions are pitiable indeed; nothing compares to the reality of the mind. Therefore, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth; the sun, moon, and stars;
humans, animals, grasses, and shrubs—all manifest their marks and characteristics based upon this reality. Now, as for the meaning of "reality":
This is precisely the pure gate of great liberation of the Buddhas and Patriarchs above. It simply depends on how each individual practices.
Whether one has practiced goodness for a single lifetime, for many lifetimes, or for immeasurable kalpas, the distinct and superior fruits of such merit manifest clearly before one.
Conversely, for those who have practiced what is not good, their lack of goodness...
The realms of experience also constantly manifest with vivid clarity; believe this! The retribution for good and evil is without the slightest deviation.

For instance, when members of the monastic community approach a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and, over a long period, cultivate a single piece of authentic mind and body to investigate the great matter of their own person, there is no reason why it should not be successfully accomplished.
Therefore, from the Buddhas and Patriarchs of old down to the elder masters of the world—
Furthermore, there is nothing that is not revealed through reality. Have you not seen how Shushan A-shi-shu, while under the guidance of Master Weishan, heard him address the assembly, saying:
"Traveling monks must truly sleep amidst sounds and forms, and sit or lie down amidst sounds and forms, only then will it be so.
At that time, Shushan stepped forward and asked: "What is the phrase that does not fall into sounds and forms? Weishan—
Shanshu held up his whisk. Shushan said, "This is a phrase that falls into sound and form. Thereupon, Weishan returned to his quarters.
Shushan felt no resonance with this and took his leave of Xiangyan. Xiangyan asked, "Why do you not stay for a while? Shushan replied, "I have no affinity with the Master.
Xiangyan asked, "What is the reason for this lack of resonance? Try reciting it for me. Shushan then recounted the previous conversation.
Xiangyan said, "I have a saying. Shushan asked, "What do you say? Xiangyan said, "When words are uttered, they are not sounds;

before form appears, there is no object. Shushan said, "So, there is someone here after all. He then instructed Xiangyan, saying, "Brother, when you have a place to dwell in the future, I shall come to see you.
If you people wish to recognize this "when words are uttered, they are not sounds; before form appears, there is no object," [you must look closely].
"Ma! This is precisely what the Old Man Śākyamuni meant when he said: "When one person awakens to reality and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions completely vanishes.
Even the light of a firefly is like this. Since Xiangyan has already scratched Shushan’s itchy spot, it is not only Baizhang who must inspect him;
even the venerable masters of great insight throughout the ages will not let him off the hook. Baizhang—
When it grew late at Mount Shishen, Guishan asked Xiangyan about the matter of sound and form: "Is that short *ācārya* still here? Xiangyan replied, "He has already departed.
Guishan said, "What did you say to him? Xiangyan said, "I once spoke with him as well. Guishan said, "Try to repeat it for me.
Xiangyan said, "'Speech issues forth, yet it is not sound; before forms appear, there is no object. Guishan asked, "What did he say?"
Yan said, "He deeply approved. Guishan laughed and said, "I thought this short fellow had some long-range merit;
it turns out he is merely stuck here. Observe this move by Guishan—it truly startles heaven and shakes the earth.
It is a pity that the land is vast and people are few. Guishan spoke again: "If this boy has a place to settle in the future, it will be near a mountain, but not one with..."
Burning firewood. Being near water yet having no water to drink. There are thorns within the soft mud. Yet the words of the ancients must surely not be false.
In the world today, to seek out one who speaks words that do not arise from sound or form, and who does not conform to things, is just like digging through the earth to find the sky;
how much more so when it comes to wanting to understand the speech of Guishan? It goes without saying. Nevertheless, take care to avoid [this pitfall].
"Drilling through tortoise shells and striking tiles"—fundamentally, for a great master to occupy the curved bamboo seat is no small matter.

Since I first entered the world, wherever I have resided, it has not been that I have failed to stir up and clarify this matter for my brothers; yet I have never once touched upon its very core point.
Recently, while residing at Jianfu, two or three hundred patch-robed monks happened to gather together, and because of that, I briefly...

Exposing their sharp edges, they have consequently stirred up boundless waves of turmoil. Since then, they have consistently acted according to circumstances, never selling pearls as if they were peas.
The ancients had the saying, "Seeing the worthy, one thinks of emulating them.
In these days, the time since the Sage has long passed; the errors and delusions of false teachers are not the fault of sentient beings. This is the true nature of those who follow the Way. To act...
One who applies effort investigates only beneath their own heels. Pushing and pushing until they suddenly reach the bottom, are they not a person of great power?
Even if they have not yet reached the bottom, their words and meaning will be lively and free-flowing; they will never become idle chatter or worldly talk.
The speech of goblins and demons; the speech of false teachers’ seals of certification; the speech of those who claim to have a "place of seeing";

the speech of those who know such matters—these are all forcibly cast into the pit of birth-and-death, annihilation, and permanence. As it is said: "A true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is a great causal condition."
This old monk traveled on pilgrimage, traversing Jiangxi and Hunan until he reached the forge of the venerable Master Yuanwu.
There, he could not open his mouth again; it was just like trying to catch a sparrow while sitting on the ground. That master did not strike out recklessly when acting for others;
once he did strike, he was steep and abrupt, leaving no room for people to find a foothold. Later, when I arrived at the place of my former teacher, it was somewhat...
Once I understood that contact is pure, I finally saw clearly the words of my late teacher, Master Yuanwu.

For the patriarchs who served as guides for others, such individuals have been difficult to find throughout antiquity and the present; their fundamental methods were utterly distinct from those teachers who merely mixed mud and water.
How could these two possibly be spoken of as being on the same level? Formerly, Chan Master Ren of Baishui at Gaoyang addressed the assembly, saying:
"I generally do not wish to dally with people’s sons and daughters before sound or after words.
Why is this? It is because sound is not sound, and form is not form. At that time, a monk asked: "What is meant by 'sound is not sound'? Ren replied: "To call it..."
"Can it be called 'form'? The monk said, "What is form that is not form? Ren said, "Can it be called 'sound'? The monk bowed.
Ren said, "Tell me, did I speak for you, or did I answer your question? If you can see it here, you will understand what Guishan meant when he said:
'This short fellow thought there was something special about him; it turns out he was just right here. This little bit of clarity."
[The Master] said, "I have just seen Master Baisui Ren say: 'Let me tell you—my answers for you do not fail to penetrate to the very top and the very bottom.
When a sharp-witted person hears such a statement, it is not merely like pouring *amṛta* (clarified butter) upon their crown.
If this is not yet the case, you must practice authentically and realize authentically. King Yama does not fear much talk. [I shall now] take my leave."
The donor Zhang Ziming, having prepared an image of the Buddha for a celebratory repentance ceremony, requested a small-scale discourse (*xiaocan*). Addressing the assembly, he said:

"The secret words of the Tathāgata have never been concealed; they reveal the essence directly and without partiality, manifesting it right before one's eyes. Yet, as for this entire Great Canon of the Teachings—from where has it come?
Unless one possesses the eye atop the crown of the head and the talisman behind the elbow, how could one ever penetrate and clarify this single point?"
Right now, sitting and standing with solemn dignity, each of you stands upon the earth with your heads toward heaven, teeth clenched and hair upon your heads.
How would you explain this principle that has never been concealed from the beginning? Is it movement and stillness, knowing the past and foretelling the future?
Is it bowing, turning, looking down, and looking up, pervading all places? Is it a single word or a single silence?

To sit, lie down, talk, and laugh—this is it? If you take this to be something that can be uncovered or revealed, it is no different from seeking a seam in a drawn sword, or beating out foam from a fire.
Little do you realize that this is precisely the frantic activity of karmic consciousness, having no fundamental basis to rely upon.
Have you not seen how Master Changsha said: "Those who study the Way do not recognize the Real, because they have only recognized the spirit from of old"?
The root of birth and death throughout immeasurable kalpas—fools call this the "original person. These ancients saw through the Tathāgata’s secret words until they were entirely free of doubt;
when they casually brought forth a single pivot or displayed a single realm, there was nothing that did not penetrate to the very top and bottom.
They never again fell into delusion within the shell of dreams and illusions, nor did they ever force artificiality upon the fleshly heart-mind.
Furthermore, there was a monk who asked an ancient worthy: "When a student has a question while staying with you, Master, how do you deal with it?

The ancient worthy replied: "Even if there were one, I would cut it into three pieces. Observe this man who has attained the Way; when he brings forth [his realization], it is truly brilliant and majestic.
Has there ever been even a single thread’s worth of rational argument offered to students? It is simply dry and parched, like a single Mount Sumeru;
all the worldly conditions of favor and adversity cannot shake it, and the causes and conditions of good and evil have no way to encompass it.
Is this not a true Great Man, a man of the Way beyond the ordinary? I venture to ask:
Friends, consider this: when the Old Śākyamuni had not yet entered his mother’s womb, where did his thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics come from?

If you can see through this point, you will then see the great-hearted donor Zhang Ziming, together with his wife Zhao, at the very moment their initial thought arose as they adorned the image of the Old Śākyamuni.
As for Subhūti’s very first thought before he had even begun his preparations—where was Śākyamuni, the Old Man, at that moment?
You must by all means avoid making strange fabrications within the shell of dreams and illusions, or upon the fleshly lump of the mind-consciousness.
At this point, do not ask what Śākyamuni, the Old Man, was like; simply and directly bring this very first thought to an end.
If one contemplates this thoroughly, it is not that which was before entering the mother’s womb; it is not that which is after entering the mother’s womb;
it is not that which comes out from the mother’s womb; it is not something molded; it is not something assembled; it is not the very first thought-moment;
nor is it that which remains after the first thought-moment has ceased. Then, Zhang Ziming and his wife Zhao...

[The Master] said: "Master Mr. Zongchao, along with your entire family and retinue—since you have already realized that from the very beginning there is nothing at all, where then could you possibly meet the Old Śākyamuni?
Do you understand this clearly? 'Offer this body and mind to every dust mote of a land;
this is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness. [He gave a shout. He descended from his seat.

After the informal sermon (xiaochan), he again cited Mingxi’s instruction to the assembly, saying: "I have a great illness, which cannot be cured by worldly physicians. Observe how this ancient master revealed such a message;
it was truly brilliant and magnificent. In reality, there was nothing else to it: he simply stepped upon the pivotal mechanism of the ultimate realm.
Once brought forth, it encompassed heaven and embraced earth, such that none could approach it. This was his way from days of old.
There was one who possessed true understanding. Later, a monk held this question up to Caoshan, asking, "I do not yet know what kind of illness this is.
Caoshan, knowing exactly where the monk’s intent lay, immediately said, "It is the illness of being unable to gather [the mind]. This man was truly one who possessed understanding.

How could he be compared to those nowadays who have no grounding and speak recklessly at will; as soon as they see someone ask, "I do not yet know what kind of illness this is," they immediately launch into [their own fabrications].
Within this tangle of vines, it is just like being dragged through a saw; you pull it away, and I drag it back—when will it ever come to rest?
What has this to do with the primary matter of one's own practice? Everyone has this kind of ailment; they simply do not recognize that they are ill.
It is truly impossible to gather [the mind) together. Since they do not recognize their illness, it becomes a chronic malady, and once it has become so...
This is simply the frantic activity of karmic consciousness, having no fundamental basis to rely upon. When the year comes to its end and the cycle is exhausted, there is nowhere to find strength;
is this not tragic? If you can step upon this ailment that cannot be gathered or assembled, you will have the means to transcend birth and escape death.
This monk asked again, "Do all sentient beings also have this ailment? The Master said, "They do."
The monk said, "Since you have it, why are you not ill? Cao Shan said, "If sentient beings were ill, they would no longer be sentient beings.
This monk was also capable of investigating the matter. He then asked, "Does Master Cao Shan also have this illness?
Cao Shan said, "I am currently searching for its point of origin and cannot find it. This statement is indeed steep and perilous; how could it possibly not be Cao Shan?

How can one even open one’s mouth? Although one truly cannot find its point of origin, those throughout the lands who possess correct knowledge and correct view cherish and nurture it as a sublime secret for transcending the world;
they are unwilling to casually reveal it to others.
If you were under the gate of Jianfu Monastery, this would be precisely a great illness—what is called the "sweatshirt against the flesh," what is called the "deep pit of liberation."
It is also called "dead water," it is also called "ink juice," and it is also called "clear understanding.
You all, if you fall ill to the point where you cannot find its origin, simply come and ask Jianfu; I shall reveal it for you. What can the various quarters do to you? Why?
It is precisely because of this illness. This monk asked again: "Do all the Buddhas also have this?"
“Is there sickness? Shanshan said. A monk asked, “Why is he not sick? Shanshan replied, “Because he is alert and aware. This old man was a direct successor of the Cao-Dong school.
He possessed the skillful means of mutual interplay and indirect engagement that avoids transgression;
he attained great mastery in all eight directions when facing critical situations. How could he merely guard the old ruts and blind the eyes of students? You practitioners, since you have come here—
Gather together. Throughout the two periods of day and night, exert yourselves with all your vigor; time does not wait for man.
Even Confucian scholars say, "If one hears the Way in the morning, it is acceptable to die in the evening," how much more so for a monk?
The Preceptor of the Temple of the Transmission of the Dharma (Chōbō-ji), Chitō, requested the Master of Ringing the Bell to address the assembly, saying:
"Rough copper and dull iron, beautiful jade and refined gold—all are cast from a single mold in the great forge and red furnace.
They do not require the supernatural power of Vaiśravaṇa Deva, nor are they brought down from the summit of Mount Sumeru. Their value as vessels is profound."
A thousand *jin* [of weight]; a tower a hundred feet high. To open the Samādhi of Universal Penetration and emit the pure, wondrous sound:

you must directly take responsibility through the faculty of sight; do not seek to comprehend it through the ears. The boiling cauldrons and glowing coals will extinguish themselves without being blown upon;

the mountains of knives and trees of swords will collapse without waiting for a shout. Dull dreams are instantly dispelled, and delusion is fully awakened to. The myriad phenomena and the ten thousand forms—*sanluo*.
All perform the dance; throughout the trichiliocosm, the great assembly hears it all at once. But tell me, where does the final stroke fall?
Even kalpa-stones may wear away, yet the profound resonance has no end.
The Recorded Sayings of Master Ying’an, Volume Six;
The Recorded Sayings of Master Ying’an, Volume Seven.
Compiled by his Dharma-heir disciples, including Shouquan, et al.
The Dharma words above were shown to the Chan practitioner Wei.

When Bodhidharma came from the West, he pointed directly to the human mind so that one might see one's nature and become a Buddha; this was indeed straightforward, essential, and concise—a true eye of correct vision.
It appears that things have already gone seven steps wrong and eight steps astray. Having no other recourse, I shall treat this like a dead horse with medicine.
This very mind of direct pointing is precisely where the Yellow-Faced Old Man failed for forty-nine years despite his horizontal and vertical explanations;
it is most refined and most wondrous. Rarely has anyone reached this true pulse. This mind cannot be transmitted through words; it can only be...
Self-realization and self-awakening reach the state where there is neither delusion nor awakening; it is simply the ordinary act of wearing clothes and eating food.
There is no longer any need for these manifold esoteric interpretations and intellectual paths to clutter the breast.

Vast and spacious, serene and at ease—when the Patriarch said that with a single even-mindedness all is naturally exhausted, only then does one attain great utility. This remains so even when facing the moment of birth and death; it is profoundly still.
In profound stillness, there is not even a hair’s breadth of movement; it is simply like this, as if sitting atop Mount Sumeru.
Is this not what is required? In recent years, though the brothers who study the Way call themselves "traveling monks," they are just like cold water poured upon stone.
Wherever they go to register their stay, they do nothing but harbor deluded thoughts and memories, using the contesting of victory and defeat to pass for equanimity.
How truly pitiable! If one were a person of the true cause traveling on foot, one would never act in such a manner.
Observe how the sages of antiquity, carrying their bundles, emerged from the monasteries and entered the communities;
they drew near to authentic spiritual friends for ten or twenty years, then withdrew to examine themselves, like cold ashes or withered wood, diligently investigating the very root and foundation.

A few words: you must first reach the point of true reality before you can follow conditions with effortless spontaneity; only then are you called a "monk who has accomplished his task" or a "high-ranking traveler.
If your mind-ground is not thoroughly clear and bright, how can you bring to rest the thoughts and mental stirrings that arise throughout the twelve periods of the day?
They swirl about like thousands of waves and ten thousand billows—how can they be dissolved away? When you arrive at this point...
If there is no point of breakthrough, one is merely a thief who knows nothing and steals the food of the Sangha;
Linji Master called such a person a "shaved soldier. Coming and going in cycles of plundering, they rob themselves until their entire body is nothing but bare bone.
Suddenly, when conditions cease, all the wit, ingenuity, and sharp intelligence one has possessed throughout life will not serve one in the slightest at the moment the light of the eyes falls.
Even if one has accomplished karmic deeds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges over many lifetimes, it will only further delay the opportunity to transcend birth and death.
One may obtain only the blessings and rewards of gods and humans; once these rewards are exhausted, one will remain as before with no way out.
If you wish to exhaust the void of kalpas and reach the end of the future, so that your enjoyment is never-ending, you must directly realize the emptiness of the mind.

Since you have not yet been able to thoroughly verify this Way, you must receive the great vows of the ancients, select a master of the fundamental school, cast aside your formal robes, and exhaust this present retribution.

If one exhaustively investigates this koan with the whole body, there will be none who fail to achieve realization. However, I fear that you may treat it as if it were merely something to be preserved or lost;
though you speak of practicing Chan on your lips, within your belly you are entirely unwilling to do so.

If this is the case, it would be better to return to a single point and look at the teachings with sincere devotion, performing pure deeds so that you will not lose your human form in the future. As an ancient worthy said: "To speak for ten zhang is not as good as..."

To practice even for an inch is correct. Furthermore, today monasteries stand facing one another, and they call themselves the transmission of the Heart-Essence of Direct Pointing by those who are "Good Friends" (kalyāṇamitra).
But ultimately, how is this mind transmitted? What is its form?

Lately, a certain class of demons has emerged—what the scriptures call "evil friends"—each offering divergent interpretations under the guise of benefiting others, or perhaps providing mere indications and teachings.
When people rest and find relief, they must not engage in any deliberation at all. As soon as a thought arises, it must be immediately eliminated.
Some teach that one should remain perpetually without affairs, neither burning incense nor prostrating in worship.

Others insist on making people investigate the past and present, which is just like a pedantic, self-made lecturer. Still others take the sincere heart of the ancient masters of old to provide direct guidance.
This is called "establishing the gate and courtyard. Perhaps, when a student of the house (a master) comes to the room, [the teacher] utters a phrase that seems similar;
after beating him for half a day and asking another question, the student offers a further response that happens to hit the mark.
Then, [the teacher] says, "This brother has found a point of entry. But tell me, what kind of people does this benefit? Does it accord with the Direct Pointing?
"Is it the mind? It is certainly not a single speck of connection. This is why Master Fojian said:
"Most of the present-day spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) point crookedly to the human mind, claiming that by speaking of nature one becomes a Buddha"—this is precisely what he meant.
The true lineage of Linji has been passed down from Baizhang at Master Mazu’s shout to the present day; it is not merely a matter of the realization and certification of the various great patriarchs.

The life-root (*jīvitendriya*) likewise thoroughly realizes the life-vein of Buddhas and Patriarchs—unspeakably, unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeyas—without the slightest deviation, not even as much as a hair’s breadth. Baizhang received it from Huangbo; Huangbo received it from Linji;
Linji transmitted it to Sansheng, who said: "Who knows that my treasury of the true Dharma-eye has been extinguished within this blind donkey? It is precisely this...
If one can see through this saying, how could there still be a Linji school? Master Degui followed me out of a sense of dharma and righteousness;
he pursues the ancient style with tireless diligence, exhaustively investigating the matter beneath the monastic robe. Truly, this may be called "truly not traveling in vain.
If you wish to understand it easily, simply look at the very place where thoughts arise and movements of mind occur throughout the twelve periods of the day. Just...

At that very moment, this stirring thought is suddenly and directly cleared away; it is utterly ungraspable, like the great void, yet even the form and segments of the void do not exist. Inside and outside are as one; both the realm of wisdom and its objects are extinguished, and all subtle understandings vanish. The three periods of time are equal. Reaching this stage is called being an "unlearned, non-active person of the leisurely Way. Furthermore, one must know what the Fifth Patriarch spoke of: "Even if you have attained the Way, you must not dwell upon it; If you dwell upon it, you will fall into the pit of views.

If you do not dwell upon it, you will become a Buddha; If you dwell upon it, you will become a demon. This is what he meant. It is said: "The Way is originally without words; it is only because of deluded thoughts that we speak of it.

If you can cut off deluded thoughts at their root, there is nothing further to be done. This is the ultimate point. One must also know that there is a verse by the Sixth Patriarch: "The Way has no difficulty; Only fear attachment to words. Directly point to the human mind; See one's nature and become a Buddha. This is the final instruction. If you can understand this, you will not be far from the Way. If you cannot, you must continue to practice diligently. Do not merely seek for it in books or rely on intellectual understanding; you must realize it within yourself. Only then will you be free from birth and death. This is the true teaching of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Do not let it pass in vain. Go and practice it! Go and practice it!
Finally attained. Since the Venerable One had offered incense with sincere devotion, I have therefore written this and entrusted it to him for his journey.
On the full moon day of the eighth month in the eleventh year of the Shaoxing era, shown to the practitioner Xi.

In ancient times, when elder practitioners of long-standing realization first resolved their minds to travel as pilgrims, it was because the two characters for "birth and death" had not yet been resolved.
They would journey tens of thousands of *li* to seek true and virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) in order to gain definitive discernment regarding this matter.

For ten or twenty years, they would set aside all worldly trifles and curiosities, keeping this [truth] ever-present in their minds. Not for even a single moment did they fail to remain within its sphere; yet they still feared that they might stray.
"If one cannot accomplish this matter, it will not be resolved. For twenty years, Master Changqing traveled back and forth between Xuefeng and Xuansha, wearing out six or seven meditation cushions.
Is this not proof that even those of great capacity could not yet attain thorough realization?

This is because the ancients, in their study of the Way, would not settle for minor achievements; they were determined that if they could not realize it in this very life, they would simply stop. Ultimately...
I did not dare to accept this casually. Alas! It was profoundly difficult to realize. One day, seeing the curtain being drawn back, it was suddenly as if a lacquer bucket were shattered;
the very root of my life was severed with a snap. Thereupon, I spoke this verse: "How very strange! How very strange!
When the curtain is rolled up, one sees the whole world. If someone asks me what school I understand, I take up my whisk and strike them right on the mouth!"

This is precisely the mind that Bodhidharma pointed directly to. Without even a hair’s breadth of conceptual grasping, intellectual understanding, or awakening, one may then be considered a seedling of the Buddha-dharma.
Whenever I see my fellow practitioners nowadays applying themselves to their practice, they are never in a state of sinking or agitation; instead, they remain seated in a state of mere alertness.
Within this ground, if one is subject to sinking or agitation, it is like a drunken person walking a long road.

If one indulges in a state of mere alertness, then sensory perceptions will escape into the heart and viscera, taking them to be the ultimate Dharma. One must simply abandon these two divergent paths and bring them to a single point;
by constantly maintaining this mindful alertness, there will come a moment of sudden, thorough penetration. This is not something extraordinary.
Lately, there has been a certain class of practitioners in the monastic communities who do not personally engage in the authentic practice of their own lives.

They stubbornly cling to the masters' talk about the "sicknesses of Chan," yet how could Chan ever have any sickness? It is simply because they have grasped the teachings in a haphazard manner and take mere rote memorization to be the ultimate truth.
Consequently, they find no real power within their fundamental study; for this reason, the masters of our school employ [the following methods].
There are some who take the basic fodder of their own station as "untying the sticky and removing the bonds," causing students to recognize what is not so;
yet they instead consume the words of the Master used to treat their illnesses, taking them into their hearts as the ultimate Dharma. This is truly pitiable.
Now, if you wish for this matter to be easily accomplished, simply maintain a state of mind that is free from distraction, pure and single-mindedly true, for a long time.
This is naturally to penetrate to the very source and bottom of the Dharma.

To show the initial transformation of Guoqing, the ancient practitioners of the Way have deeply lamented that birth and death remain unclarified; they established great vows as firm as metal and stone, casting off all attachments wherever they were encountered.
To seek the true and authentic spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) for the sake of resolving this great matter of one's existence prior to birth—how could this be undertaken lightly?
It requires passing twenty or thirty years, exhausting all攀緣 (*pān-yuan*, objective attachments) and extinguishing all 意想 (*yi-xiang*, conceptual thoughts).

With diligent effort in the cold, silent state, one day there is a sudden breakthrough, like a lacquer bucket falling. One loses the shadows and glimmers before one’s eyes; this must surely be the offering from the past.
The furniture of ghosts—deities that rely upon grass and cling to wood—all melts away like ice and crumbles like tiles.
It is entirely one’s own native ground and natural radiance. Like a long sword leaning against the heavens, who would dare look it directly in the eye?
To look is to go blind. Therefore, when entering the gate, Linji immediately shouts; Deshan immediately strikes with his staff; and Luzu, upon seeing a monk, turns his face to the wall. All are thus.

When I saw the monk raise his finger, I thought of those from the patriarchs down—whether Buddhas or Ancestors, or any old masters in the world who possess the "eye"—who entirely employ the fodder of one's own fundamental portion to hold one up face-to-face, like a blade that severs the life-force.

If one is a person who recognizes the sensation of pain, they will immediately know where it lands. But as for those who have no blood beneath their skin and no pearl in their eyes—for them, let alone...
I leave it for Maitreya to descend and explain its refutation to others.

To the Chan practitioner Shi-Zhan, I show that beneath the Gate of Manifest Fruit there is no Chan to be taught and no Way to be transmitted; there is only a single sword, which does not spare even the Buddha.
Whether you be an ancestor, a sage, or an ordinary person, as soon as you raise [your hand], I shall strike you down.
If you can turn your body beneath the edge of the sword, you may go forth at will from one monastery into another community; I shall then apply pressure to this old fellow on the meditation seat.
If you see water dripping from your mouth, pack your bag and go; would that not be most joyful?
Yet, if you have not yet attained thorough realization and can only carry the burden, you must not be careless; you should be profoundly meticulous. As Zen Master Ying of Shending said:
"Study must be real study, and realization must be real realization; King Yama does not fear much talk."
I have not failed the original vow of my lifelong journey as a wandering monk. Having relied upon a man of true substance for nearly twenty years, I have exhausted this retribution-body;
yet suddenly, I have encountered his lethal hand. The crown of my head has split open, my eyes have fallen out, and all my skills and arts have been stripped away.
Vibrant and agile, shouting "ta-ta" and "ya-ya" like a lion king, moving and dwelling with freedom and roaring with mastery—
is this not the spirit of a great man? Only by performing the deeds of a great man can one be called an extraordinary and preeminent figure among the masses.
Master Baiyun Yuan said, "Once you have attained awakening, you must meet the right person;

if you do not meet such a person, you are merely a tailless monkey that people laugh at as soon as it is brought out for display. Those who have deep faith in this Way are one in ten thousand—it is truly pitiable."
To the Chan practitioner Qing and his fellow monks who have gone forth from the ranks:
Even before the Yellow-Faced Old Man emerged from his mother’s womb, he had already used a single broken trailing rope to pierce the nostrils of all people under heaven;
when he finally appeared in the world, he continued to use that same rope for forty-nine years, with his mouth flapping away.
It is simply this very thread. It is also said that for forty-nine years he never uttered a single word; it was simply this very thread.
At the end, when the flower was held up and Kāśyapa smiled, the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye was entrusted to Mahākāśyapa—this too was simply this very thread.
Since the branching of the schools until the present day, [the masters] have been forging Buddhas and refining [the teachings].
The Patriarch used only this "seeking-line" (zōso). Lately, however, one looks at this seeking-line and sees that no one knows how to handle it.
Even if there were someone who could handle it, it would be like reaching out one's hand in the dead of night to seize an object;

though one grasps the object, one knows not whether it is blue, yellow, red, or white, long, short, large, or small—it is utterly indistinct. Why is this? It is because the point of origin has not been correctly discerned.

Consequently, one ends up muddled and confused. If you were to examine the matter with precision regarding where this comes from, you would see that the Buddhas of the three periods of time speak dreams, the six generations of patriarchs speak dreams, and the old monks of the world speak dreams.
They dream that the Yellow-Faced Old Man has lost his tethering rope. Now that it is lost, tell me, you people, what will you use for sustenance? This little bit!
It is like a vast iron net stretching across the heavens. Those who can penetrate it find an open path in all eight directions;
those who cannot must beg for their lives from the hands of you superior men.
Shi Chong, the attendant, presented the recorded sayings of Master Kaiyuan:

"The Patriarch came from the West to point directly to the human mind, so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha. Within the school of the patch-robed monks, this is like digging a hole to bury someone alive.
Having no other recourse, I shall treat it as a dead horse. I will speak of the Buddha; I will speak of the Patriarchs."
To speak of "mind" and speak of "nature" is like the saying of exchanging a honeyed fruit for a bitter gourd.

If one is a true man of great capacity, they will cut through it with a single stroke; retreating to themselves, they look through with sudden clarity into their original face before a single thought has arisen.
When the ten voids are thoroughly illumined and the state is vast and unimpeded, one is then identical to Śākyamuni Buddha.
They are not distinct. This is called the Samādhi of the Crown King; it is called the Mass of Blazing Flames;
it is called the Vajra King’s Precious Sword; it is called the Crouching Lion; it is called the Poison-Smeared Drum—it has various such names. At such a time, who is there for birth and death?
Who is there for coming and going? Who is there for good and evil? Who is there for opposition and compliance? Who is there for right and wrong?
Who is there for heaven or hell? Who is there for the four modes of birth and the six paths of existence? The entire earth is this very gate of liberation;
the whole body is the object of enjoyment of the "Person of No-Rank. Have you not seen how Master Linji said:
"Upon the mass of bare flesh, there is a Person of No-Rank who constantly enters and exits through the gates of the faces of all of you? Not yet?
"Look at the evidence! At that moment, a monk stepped forward. Linji rose from his meditation seat, grabbed him by the chest, and held him fast, saying, "Speak quickly!
Speak quickly! The monk hesitated. Linji pushed him away and said, "What is the 'true person of no station'? It is a dried-up shit-stick!"
This is precisely the lineage of Bodhidharma. When Linji attained this samādhi, he was like a great rain cloud or hundreds of thousands of millions of thunders;
his transformations were beyond compare, and his proclamation grew ever loftier. When Sansheng attained this samādhi, his response became ever more sublime.
This extended to Xinghua, Nanyuan, Shoushan, Fengxue, Fenyang, Ciming, Yangqi, Baiyun, Dongshan, and so forth.
Both Mount Yuanwu and [Zhaozhou] attained the true lineage of Linji; they saw through to their original mind and mastered its wondrous samādhi.

Truly, it can be said that they did not fail the essential point of the "separate transmission outside the teachings" that points directly at the human heart. It was from this elder Cigan that the great resolve first arose to travel abroad for study.
At the beginning, he visited Master Yuanwu at Mount Jiangshan to realize this samādhi. He kept it deeply concealed among the masses for over twenty years;

no one had yet been able to discern and bring it forth. This was because throughout his life, he had attained a thorough realization that transcended the ordinary, and his practice was so stable and secure that he could not easily be hurried by a single word or phrase into seeking recognition from others. During the fourth and fifth years of the Shaoxing era, this...
The samādhi is revealed; its radiance illuminates the world like the great sun-disk ascending into the vast void.
Those with eyes behold this radiance as pure, indestructible, and unmixed. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth rely upon this radiance to bring forth all things;
the sun, moon, and stars rely upon this radiance to shine brightly through the darkness; and hell and heaven rely upon this radiance.
Clearly abiding in good and evil, all moving beings rely upon this radiance to emerge and submerge.

Monks rely upon this radiance to open the great furnace and forge the world, using the tongs and hammer to shatter the nests of sages and ordinary folk, and sever the life-root of Buddhas and patriarchs.
Once the life-root is severed, one seeks the place from which this radiance comes, but it is utterly unattainable. — Master Panshan.
The moon of the Way-mind is solitary and full; its light swallows the myriad forms. The light does not illuminate objects, nor do objects exist.
When both light and objects have vanished, what is this thing? Master Yunmen said, "The entire earth is light—what do you call 'self'?
If you can recognize this light, then objects cannot be found either; what use is there for this dung-light and objects? Since light and objects...
It cannot be grasped; what kind of thing could it possibly be? When one studies the Way and flows toward this state, how can one provide a standard for support?
If you are one who has smashed the lacquer bucket, you will immediately know where the two elders fell. Once you know where the two elders fell, tell me:
are they within the light, or are they not within the light? If you say they are within the light, Yunmen also said: "What is there?"
The realm of "ma shi" light. If you say that [the Way] does not reside within the light, Panshan also said, "Light swallows the myriad phenomena. Therefore it is said:

after breaking through the lacquer bucket, one must encounter a person before one can succeed. If you do not encounter such a person, even upon reaching this point, you will lose the eye for penetrating the barrier.
However, if you have broken through the lacquer bucket and have already passed through the forge of a master of the true lineage, [you are ready].
When one emerges like refined gold of a hundred smeltings, like a fierce tiger with wings outspread, or like a golden-winged garuḍa swallowing a dragon,
only then may one be called a true scion of the lineage of the Dharma King.
It is shown that although the Great Sui Master previously attended more than seventy spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), those who possessed the "great eye" were only one or two;
all the others possessed right knowledge and vision (*samyagjñānadarśana*). Xianglin served Yunmen as an attendant for eighteen years.
Every single word or half-phrase recorded here beneath this paper and cloth serves as a testament to the profound sincerity with which the ancients pursued the Dharma.
When one reaches the point of penetration, it is brilliantly manifest, utterly transcending the snares of conceptual frameworks and the realm of intellectual understanding—both internal and external.
This is what is meant by the lion king’s roar, which is never in vain. In recent times, the illness of the Zen school has been its lack of vigor; where does this sickness lie? It lies in...
Regarding the point where one lacks self-confidence: first, from what does this illness arise? It arises, in fact, from an incorrect foundation (*bhūmi*).
Since the foundation is incorrect, even if one has entered a monastic community (*saṃghārāma*), one regards the community as merely a way-station;
though one speaks of and hears about *chan* (meditation), it is like a duck hearing thunder. By citing these two points, we also see the difference between people of today and those of antiquity.
This is a contradiction. Yet, were it not for the occasion of striking the square with the crooked, one would never have known the profound debt of gratitude owed to the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
thus, we know that the two great masters were not mistaken.
Shi Zhang was a genuine practitioner of the Way whose nature had long been imbued with the seed-wisdom of Prajñā. As soon as he emerged, his spirit was firm and upright;
from the very first step, he stood out preeminent and transcendent, unlike those who are merely common. Indeed, he was one who had personally approached the truth at its ultimate level.
A true master of the orthodox lineage never utters a single word or phrase that is false or extravagant.
Yet, this matter cannot be approximated by intellectual understanding or views; how could it ever be mimicked by worldly wisdom or clever eloquence?
Therefore, Luoshan said: "When a man of superior capacity first steps through the gate, he immediately knows the essential principle, yet he still fears the old fellow on the rope bed."
The Han is dozing off; turn your head back and take another look.

If you are a true adept, even while temporarily hanging up your jar and bowl, you must fear that the old man on the rope bed has not yet awakened from his slumber and has water dripping from his mouth. This is no place to moor your boat;
go instead to stay overnight at a layperson’s house. Observe how that person who has penetrated to the bottom suddenly reveals a message, making it so that even Heaven—
For the inferior monk, there is not even a thread’s breadth of a place to settle; nor is he permitted to dwell upon it.

This lack of a path for settling is what is called the "method of driving the plow and seizing the food. Truly appearing once in an age, how could this be something to be mixed with mud and water by the common crowd, thereby blinding the eyes of those who study?
It is shown that from the time of Śākyamuni— the one with the rounded head— prior to him, down through the Great Mirror of Caoxi and all the great patriarchs since then,
there has been a direct succession and a subtle, secret accord that does not transcend the person themselves, whether in the midst of the twelve hours of daily life, in every movement or stillness.

If, between a single word and a single silence, you can indeed remain undeluded regarding your original resolve and suddenly perceive the natural radiance of your fundamental ground right here and now,
then you will walk hand-in-hand with the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity, sharing the same experience and upholding the lineage of the thousand sages.

Unable to reach its depths even when approached closely, it is that toward which the myriad spirits look up in reverence. At the place where there is no door, one must grasp the single stroke upon the crown of the head.

Not only does this liberate all people from their adhesions and bonds, but it extends to the four modes of birth, the nine states of existence, and the three paths and six realms of rebirth, causing each to thoroughly realize the fundamental source.
When every individual clearly understands and possesses right knowledge and right view, is this not the accomplishment of a great man?

"This is the business of a great man. Linji said, "Twenty years ago, when I was with my late master Huangbo, I asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma three times and was beaten three times, like being brushed off with a bundle of mugwort.
Now I wish to take another beating; who will give me a hand? At that time, a monk came forward and said, "I shall give you a hand. Linji took hold of him.
Linji held out his staff and gave it to the monk. As the monk reached out to receive it, Linji struck him. Observe how he manifested this Great Dharma;
it truly transcends all schools and stands apart from the common eye.

How could it be compared to those of today who cling like grass or wood to the teachings—masterless orphan souls sitting within the eighth consciousness, measuring and judging those of the highest caliber? Their great capacity and great function are exactly like this.
Regarding the story of the fireflies burning Mount Sumeru, the Gui-zong lineage has been far too desolate for many years.
I myself am thinking that I deserve sixty blows; who will strike them? Suddenly, Upāsaka Yuan stepped forward and said, "I, Fa-yuan, shall strike them.
[Gui-zong] said to him, "Wait until you have cast the bell, and then I will hand over my staff."
In the "Chapter on Demonstrating the Construction," it is recorded that when his great-uncle Fuyan first took charge of Longmen in Huaiyou, there were only ruined buildings and a few remaining monks.

Yet, before a year had passed, men of exceptional talent from all over the world were crowding the monastery like shoes upon the floor. Within less than a few years, the entire temple was completely renovated; thus, at Dongshan—

The Way [of the Buddha] was greatly propagated throughout the world. At the end of the Jianyan era and the beginning of the Shaoxing era, the military fires had nearly annihilated both people and things;

yet only Longmen remained intact. This was because this old man possessed supreme *prajñā*-wisdom and vast vows and practices—how could the cycles of worldly existence possibly move him by even a hair’s breadth?
He once said to his disciples: "You build for me, and I shall preach for you."
Chan! I will trade my golden pellets for your clay pellets. These are fine words; they penetrate both principle and phenomena.

This is what is called the thorough integration of principle and phenomena, having fully realized that all dharmas are unborn. Although this does not involve reviling the Buddhas or scolding the Patriarchs, it is nonetheless profound.
How could the Buddhas and Patriarchs possibly leave traces before him? Although he did not employ the staff or the shout, how would one dare to apply the staff or the shout?
You should know that the Way of the late Patriarch Foyan was like the great void, beyond all measure; its profound mystery and silent stillness—how could it ever be grasped through calculation?
Therefore, if a student of the Way can see through the clay pellet, they will immediately understand the golden pellet.
As for the place where the ball falls: if you can see through the golden ball, you will know where the clay ball lands.
This is the "Blow-Off Sword" of Linji; if you handle it skillfully, great merit is achieved without effort. Should you hesitate, you cannot avoid wounding your own life.

Regarding the manifestation of governance and transformation, Master Yantou said: "In general, when proclaiming the Teaching, one must allow the three phrases to flow forth from within a state of desirelessness.
This is merely a matter of principle: biting off and biting on; wishing to leave but not leaving; wishing to stay but not staying; or at times simply not leaving at all."
"Sometimes there is a state of absolute non-abiding; truly, these words are so!

From the ancient masters who possessed the great eye of wisdom, all have attained a bit of this talk, which is why it overturns heaven and shakes the earth. In its solitary loftiness, nothing can find a foothold within it."

To touch upon the state of fundamental reality and find nothing else to grasp; to look into the midst of the favorable and the adverse and see nothing else—that is called the "nose-tip" of the patch-robed monk.
Whenever the venerable master Yuanwu instructed his students, he would say: "If I have a single word that reaches you, I, this old monk, shall personally suffer the beating of the staff.
If there is not a single word that reaches you, you will sink into hell yourself. Observe how he obtained this small measure of realization.
The matter of speaking is like a golden-winged garuḍa parting the ocean to seize and swallow a dragon directly; it is no different. It is also said:

"One who acts as a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and occupies the high seat—if they lack the eye that discerns dragons from snakes and the power to capture tigers and rhinoceroses—they will inevitably be swallowed by the awakened ones.
This is precisely how the School of the Patriarchs (Zongmen) functions. Have you not seen when Mingzhao arrived at Quan?
At the place of Elder Zhoutan, Tan said, "When one studies under a master, one must go to where the whole person is;
one must also go to where the half-person is. Mingzhao then asked, "I do not ask about where the whole person is;
what is the place of the half-person? Tan was speechless. Later, he had his junior monk ask Mingzhao instead. Mingzhao said, "If you wish to know where the half-person is..."
"What is it? He is merely a fellow playing with a lump of mud. Guizong thought Mingzhao had seen a true master and would surely have a startling phrase;
why then did he let out the howl of a wild jackal? Tell me, where does the vital point lie?"

This "Great Canon of Teachings" shown by you two transformation-monks, Moshen, was not spoken by the Yellow-Faced Old Man; this "Direct Pointing to the Human Mind" was not transmitted by Master Bodhidharma.
These two things alone will bring calamity upon the monastics of the world, who will seek life but never find it.
Born, yet seeking death, one cannot find it. While one is still deliberating, suddenly one is pushed over by another and cut in two with a single stroke, splashing blood up to the Brahma Heaven.
Even under the gate of Guizong, such a person is still one who merely scoops up the water used for washing feet;
they have not even dreamed of seeing the meaning and intent of my ancestors. Have you not seen how Linji questioned Huangbo about the very essence of the Buddha-dharma?
In summary, he was struck with sixty blows on three occasions. Having studied under Linji for a long time, Xinghua finally attained great enlightenment upon seeing Dajue remove his cassock;
he directly perceived the underlying intent behind Linji’s eating of the staff at Huangbo.
Desiring to inherit this very lineage, he possessed no other methods nor any eccentricities—only a single, resolute consistency.
The backbone stands erect. If you can penetrate the teaching, then the lives and spirits of all people throughout the entire world will be seized by the binding rope and pierced through;
there will not be a single one who slips through the net. Is this not a great man accomplishing the deeds of a great man?
Shijian Huashi was a man of extraordinary character among the elite of the monastic community. Wherever he went, he never casually disclosed news;
if he did utter even a single word or half-sentence, it was invariably for a specific reason. Although some may not have fully grasped his intent, they nonetheless received [his teachings].

People are orderly; this is because their wisdom and discernment are refined and clear, which makes it so. Only those who are utterly blind do not inquire whether something is right or wrong, but simply believe whatever is thrown at them.
When a person of status says such a person knows how to respond, they do not realize that this is precisely a business deal that results in a loss.
When Yangshan was with Baizhang, his mouth was full of chatter; Baizhang said, "In the future, you will encounter..."
When Nanquan arrived at Mount Gui, the Master said, "When you were at Baizhang, did you ask ten for every one? Yangshan replied, "I did not dare.
The Master said, "Bring me a phrase from beyond the Buddha-dharma. As Yangshan was about to open his mouth, he was shouted out.
This happened three times; each time Yangshan attempted to answer, he was shouted out. Yangshan lowered his head and wept, saying, "The former..."
The Master said to me, "As for what he will encounter later, today is precisely that moment. From then on, he resolved his mind to enter the mountains to tend cattle for three years.
One day, when Guishan entered the mountains and saw him sitting in meditation beneath a tree, he struck him on the back once with his staff.
Yangshan turned his head, and Guishan asked, "Has Jizi (Yangshan) said anything yet? Yangshan replied, "Although I have spoken, it was not..."
To put it briefly, one need not borrow another’s mouth [to speak]. Guishan said, "My son, you understand.
This is what is meant by "discerning the melody when the strings are moved" or "knowing autumn from the falling leaves. As for Linji, who received three severe blows from Huangbo;

later, when he appeared in the world and addressed the assembly, he said, "At that time, when I was with my former master, receiving those blows was like being struck by a bundle of mugwort. Generally speaking, in raising...
Only when you become like those two great elders can you truly establish a school. Consider this: what kind of matter did Linji and Yangshan accomplish when they attained awakening?
If you can examine this thoroughly, I will grant you entry into the Dharma-gate of the letter A.
To show the mind of the practitioner who undergoes transformation and edification:
its rectitude is like a taut string. In every place and at every moment, it is like a long sword leaning against the heavens.

The world’s wealth, nobility, arrogance, luxury, and the five desires—the eight winds—have no entry point to penetrate it. Fame, profit, right, and wrong, as well as the four modes of birth and nine realms of existence, cannot cage it.
It cannot be concealed. To attain this state is precisely the moment of seizing the life-root of the "Yellow-Faced Old Man" (the Buddha).

How could this be caused by the firm and steadfast vows of merely one or two lifetimes? Rather, it is because the wisdom of all seeds (*sarvabījaka-jñāna*) has been matured through refinement over accumulated kalpas;
only after passing through various hardships can one finally draw near to the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), transcending and walking alone in solitude.
It is said in antiquity that not a single dharma arises from indolence or laziness;

it is also said that only through enduring long-term diligent suffering can one achieve realization. These are words of truth, words free from deception, and words free from falsehood. If, indeed, one penetrates this all at once—
Thousands and tens of thousands cannot cage him; calling out to him, he does not turn back.
On some future day, atop a solitary peak, if he can revile the Buddhas and scold the Patriarchs, he will truly not be a disgrace.

How could one merely eat one’s fill all day long, moving in crowds and groups, prattling about this and that, without having even the slightest thought to turn the light back upon oneself to reflect? "This body of mine now consists of the four great elements—namely, hair, body hair..."
Nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, marrow, bones, brain, and filth—all these forms return to earth.
Tears, saliva, pus, blood, lymph, mucus, foam, and the large and small excretions—all these return to water. Warmth returns to fire. Movement returns to wind.
When the four great elements have each departed, where then does this illusory body reside? Herein, you must apply yourself with urgency. If you identify it as earth or water...
If you deliberate in terms of fire and wind, the Old Śākyamuni will have no chance of emerging for as many kalpas as there are motes of dust.

If you do not deliberate in terms of earth, water, fire, or wind, it is like comparing fish eyes to a bright pearl; you fail to touch either path, which is no different from trying to satisfy hunger with a painted cake.
Thirty blows—Guizong shall eat them himself; they are none of the business of the various quarters.

This one critical pivot at the crown of the head of Master Xishi is something that even the thousand sages cannot fathom. To know it through thought is the second head; to know it without thought is the third head.
The essential point lies in the person directly taking up this burden, casting off all prior scholarly interpretations and the two divergent paths of clarity and obscurity, until [one arrives].
In this state of pure nakedness, you must further turn toward that other side: seeing the Buddha and slaying the Buddha, seeing the Patriarchs and slaying the Patriarchs.
Even within the gate of the patch-robed monks, these are still matters concerning servants and slaves.

You who are great men—do not seek Chan, do not seek the Way, do not seek the mysterious, and do not seek the wondrous at the corner of the meditation seat or from the mouth of the old monk. Turn instead toward this stinking skin-bag.
Is it not also erroneous to speak of "ultimate reality"? Whenever Muzhou saw a monk, he would say, "I see a settled case;
I grant you thirty blows. Juzhi saw a monk and raised a finger; Bimozhe saw a monk and held up a fork. As for Xuansha, he had not yet reached ultimate penetration.
From the masters of antiquity down to the present, there are none who have not pointed directly at the vital core of the matter.
Like a great mass of fire, who would dare approach it? To approach it is to be scorched by its flames.

Again, like the Golden-Winged Bird (Garuda) splitting the ocean to seize and swallow a dragon without hesitation—possessing such a spirit and such heroic distinction, one may then be called a Great Man.
Do not merely cling to the limited views of a "rat" and play with a three-inch light. Wandering from door to door, when you see someone say it is good, you follow them into goodness;
when you see someone say it is evil, you follow them into evil. This is truly pitiable. One day, Magu took up his staff and went to Zhangjing;
he circumambulated the meditation seat once, shook his staff once, and stood there upright. Zhangjing said, "It is."
He did so. Furthermore, carrying his *khakkhara* staff, he went to Nanquan, circled the meditation seat once, shook the staff once, and stood there upright.
Nanquan said, "It is not so, it is not so. Gu said, "Zhangjing said it was so; why does the Master say it is not so?"
Nanquan said: "Zhangjing says, 'This is right; you are not. This is merely turned by the power of the wind and will ultimately fall into ruin.
When a student of the Way reaches this point, how can they distinguish the black from the white? If one is skilled at investigation, the good and the evil will naturally separate."
To say that Master Dharma, who manifested strict instruction and propagated the teachings, had not yet left the Western Land [India] is already the seventh and eighth error.

Since he could not remain settled, he consequently sailed across the ocean to travel through Liang and Wei. For nine years at Shaolin, he revealed his message, which is called the "Direct Transmission of the Single Lineage. Its...
The defeat becomes even more profound. When matters cannot be avoided and one is about to err, one attempts to correct the error by aligning mind with mind;
yet, from the outset, there is not even a hair’s breadth of a principle to be grasped. What is realized is merely the realization of one's own original Dharma.

Now, how can you speak of this "original Dharma"? Is it that aligning mind with mind constitutes the original Dharma? Or is it that the mind of non-attainment constitutes the original Dharma? It is neither.
"Is it that 'the mind is neither Buddha nor a thing' that constitutes the fundamental Dharma? Is it being entirely thus that constitutes the fundamental Dharma?
Or is it being entirely not thus that constitutes the fundamental Dharma? To understand it in such a way is just like carving excrement into the shape of sandalwood;

until the end of time, it will only produce the stench of filth. Even if one’s eloquence is like a cascading river and one’s spiritual acuity is like a flash of lightning, it is still nothing but this."

"Brandishing the staff to strike at the moon"—this slight matter must be understood by one who has attained awakening (*bodhi*) before its true location can be known. What is now called "awakening" is a term used to remedy inverted views (*viparyāsa*).

From the Buddhas and Patriarchs of old down to the present, they have observed that all sentient beings flow from ignorance into inversion, and from inversion into the various realms of existence (*gati*).
Since the pathhead is mistaken, they undergo changes of head and face, creating [further delusions].
The various types of karma are said to consist of turning away from awakening due to delusion.

If one has planted roots of goodness in the past, and through the words of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) the ground of one's mind opens and becomes clear, such that one perceives the original face, this is called returning from delusion and entering awakening.

Yet, when deluded, how could there ever have been a loss of even a single hair’s breadth? When awakened, how could there ever have been an addition of even a single hair’s breadth? When deluded, one is simply deluded.
Awaken to that which is awakened to; when awakening, one awakens to that which is deluded. Once awakening and delusion are thoroughly penetrated, the root of birth and death is severed.
At once, it is like a single speck of snow upon a red-hot furnace.

Whether Buddha or Patriarch, ordinary person or sage, adverse or favorable, good or evil, long or short—even reaching to gain and loss, right and wrong—none can adhere to it. Upon this non-adherence...
Attaining realization in every situation and every matter is like empty space, which contains all forms yet makes no distinctions among any objects.
It is also like empty space, which pervades all things and enters equally into all lands. In every atom and every world-system, there is entirely this great gate of liberation.
When the teachings of the Buddha and worldly dharmas are forged into a single whole, this is precisely following...
Before one first raised the intention to practice Chan, body and mind were of one piece, and within the belly there was no such abundance of evil knowledge or evil understanding.
This is what is meant by the saying: "Having awakened, one is the same as when one had not yet awakened.

Only upon reaching this state can it be called the ground of non-doubt. I have also personally explained that there are two kinds of non-doubt: seeing through one's fundamental nature to its ultimate consummation...
Because it is a state of peace and bliss, it is not spoken of; yet one still fears falling into a stagnant attachment.

There is a certain class of people who are utterly ignorant yet claim they have no doubts, asserting that from the beginning there has been no delusion and now there is no awakening. However, when pressed to explain the point where there is neither delusion nor awakening, they are unable to proceed.
Is this not being utterly ignorant while claiming to have no doubts? This is like scorched grain or withered sprouts; it severs the life-root of the Buddha and casts out the Buddha-dharma.
How can one even speak with those who treat the Buddha’s body as mere blood? Since ancient times, the venerable elders have investigated this Great Matter;
it was not a matter of ease, but was pursued with the utmost meticulousness. How could they be compared to the elders of today, who merely carry a heavy burden? Why is this so?
There are some who, having attained a mere glimpse of insight, stop there and no longer seek decisive resolution from others. When confronted by others...
