Nine years facing the wall resulted in a circuitous path; three blows received in person only served to further distance us.
Having swept away the great skillful hands of the Nāga, I know not who can continue this way of life.
Before the Hall of Wiping Eyes, Linji’s true command is carried out but halfway. He seizes upon the ailment of Buddhas and patriarchs:
"On the river, ten thousand layers of green mountains; by the water, two or three thatched huts.
In the morning, countless small boats pass by—how can they compare to this fellow holding his fishing rod?"
My thatched hut lies beneath the Purple Sky; my fertile fields border the Stone Mirror. This life shall pass according to its lot; there is no need for the money to buy a mountain.
Such an evil bhikṣu—dare anyone approach him? He recklessly burns the fires of the three poisons and exerts himself in groundless slander.
He demolished the nest of Shaoshi and swept away the barriers to vision held by the patched-robed monks; those who heard and saw him knit their brows, as if there were no one left to look up to.
Body and mind are as one, with nothing remaining outside the body; he does not aspire to become a Buddha, nor is he an ordinary person—he willingly remains in the highest prison.
A lacquer bucket. No calculating of the smallest fraction. Ten thousand ages of silver mountains and iron walls, with not another "this," "that," "who," or "what.
To say it is so is to bury the old monk alive; to say it is not is to kill Tanhui. Both darkly penetrate the two layers of the prison gates.
In a blazing fire, even a mosquito cannot hide.
Originally a monk from the village of Huangmei, I have laughed at myself since birth for being utterly incapable. Carrying a single pitcher and a single bowl, I dwell wherever conditions lead;
who would have thought that I would now continue the ancestral lamp?
Yuzhado of Pingjiang painted this portrait of the crown [of the Master’s head].

I seek a eulogy for him who sits alone upon the great square of the *paryaṅka* seat beneath withered pines, holding his staff crosswise across his lap. To say he is Ying’an is to miss his true appearance;
to say he is not Ying’an—who would be willing to take refuge in him? Entrust this to Zudo; try to settle the matter for yourself.
Xu Boshou requests a eulogy: The waves of the great ocean are vast;
the spirit of a thousand peaks is majestic. When one sits squarely at the head, they directly unfold their family style.

With a single shout, guest and host are distinguished; through the three mysteries, the true source is discerned. As for everything else, there is no need to ask; from ancient times until now, there have been only the blind and the deaf.

Like a man of the Way seeking praise, the green mountains on the riverbank come one after another in layers. The pines and bamboos atop my cottage were planted by my own hand. All day long no one comes to my thatched gate;
only when I look do I see clouds piled up before the window.
The Chan practitioner Lian Dao painted his own portrait and requested a eulogy from Ling Xingpo.
One suffers from deafness; the other suffers from muteness. The deaf man has keen hearing;
the mute man can speak. How laughable and how tragic! One must know the proper measure of propriety.

A Portrait Eulogy for the Elder Ji-bin’s Second Niece, Who Embroidered the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra The elder Ji-bin of Wu-men is nearly a hundred years of age. His frame is clear and slender, yet his conduct possesses a dignified bearing.
Her gait was as swift as the wind; her speech and laughter were never lacking in vigor. When pressed for the reason, she had no other artifice: she delighted solely in the Buddha-dharma.

She constantly associated with spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), realizing the principles of life and death beneath their words. Her family had two nieces whose virtuous bearing was exceptionally transcendent.

From childhood, he abstained from meat; morning and evening, he remained in constant silence. Arising with composure from meditative concentration, he felt deep anguish at the knots of the ten afflictions.
He manifested his great vows spanning kalpas and eons, employing the needle to bring forth the five colors and conjuring the wondrous body of Samantabhadra, which appeared as four bodhisattvas.
It pervades the empty space of the ten directions, as bright as the sun and moon raised high. How magnificent is the White Elephant King! The pack of foxes is utterly extinguished.
One should know that this wondrous excellence is not established in some other place; if one seeks it from oneself, it is like a fever arising within the sick.
This is called correct contemplation; otherwise, it is a false teaching.
Verses composed by Li Shilang, Envoy of the Palace, and sent to the Wan-shan Hermitage.
This mountain is already a superior Mount Tiantai; atop its peaks, all is vast and still as the True Eye opens.
Infinite waters and clouds find no place to settle, yet they allow the Prime Minister to sweep the ground and come forth.
Inscription on the "Greatly Hidden" Painting by Chen Zhongda The Master Who Carries the Hoe dwells in seclusion at Yunzhuang.
Bamboo huts and thatched halls overlook a small river. This very state of leisure is his true companion;
Between the human world and the heavens, there is none his equal.
In Harmony with Li the State Councilor’s Verse for the Chan Practitioner Jian:
Composed by the Layman Qingyuan on the Crown of the Head. From the very beginning, it has been vast and empty; yet one must further penetrate the ultimate barrier of our house.

Vividly alive and slippery, it is difficult to grasp or seize. When the wind rises and the grass stirs, the principle of discernment appears. At the moment of encounter, the eight directions are opened from the start.
There is no [artificial] effort. As soon as even a hair’s breadth of a mind to take or give arises, one is immediately ensnared by the false teacher.

As I bid farewell to my lay brother, I shall now calmly endure this journey upon a light boat; though I cannot help it, the official summons leaves me no choice. I look back with deep longing for the Elder to cultivate purity.
Karma. Do not let the passing of the seasons be taken lightly.
An inscription for Layman Liu Min’s “Sixth Hermitage” on West Creek, titled “A Secluded Dwelling”:
Facing the pine-window, he sits apart from the world; before his eyes, thousands of peaks of green mountains.
Layer upon layer, this birth’s peace and joy can find no equal;
the true substance of space has no boundaries. How could the concealment of the six senses ever cover it?
If you wish to hear the unperforated flute of Shaolin, it has always been played against the wind.
The Way-essence of Master Cici’s stupa is as weighty as a mountain;
his icy resolve possesses a firm governing principle. A single punch constitutes his lifelong practice—throughout the ages, there has been none like him.
Pine and bamboo stand thick and old; clouds and mountains layer upon layer. With infinite intent toward Luoyang, I face this single burner of incense.
To the practitioner Shizhi: The gate of Shaoshi is as cold as ashes; for many years not a single person has come. If you now understand how to feel shame—
How shameful! Why not apply oneself with diligent effort for once?
Cheng Zhubu and I were both born in the Guiwei year of the Chongning era. You served as a high official while I became a monk; let us both tread the path until we reach the heavens.
The Road: Together we tread upon the crown of Vairocana. For a Chan practitioner, this journey to Mei Yang is not to be shunned even at three thousand *li*;

how much less so now that the sky and rivers are about to snow? As for the way of the mind and body, it is as if— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)
Obscure! The Old Man of Mei Yang already knew this beforehand.

Beyond the wild inn and small bridge on the path where the bell was cast, at twilight when the snow was about to fall—whose ear did that single sound prick? For a thousand ages it calls out to the foolish.
Debin composed this verse upon the restoration of the Shuangyang Pagoda:
The nine-story pagoda soars beyond the azure heavens; The sacred traces of the Seven Buddhas reside above.
When the mountain is cold and the clouds are chill at midnight, One hears only the music of the immortals and the wafting scent of heaven.

Sending off a monk to beg for mats—what need is there to limit one's heart to a mere three-rafters? To penetrate directly is the single-flavored Chan of Guizong. I recall that year when he once rolled it up;
now, without cause, he unfurls it again for others to sleep upon.
Wu Bi-dong requested a small discourse, after which he spoke this verse:
At the tips of the hundred grasses lies the eye of a thousand sages; Upon the point of a single hair are ten thousand layers of barriers. There is no further Buddha-dharma nor any hidden mysteries;
Only with those who truly understand can one travel together.
I send these six practitioners of Chan to follow Elder Hong at Dazhi.

Dazhi has been desolate for a long time; it is the six superior men who shall restore it. Before the pivot of the teaching, they deploy far-reaching strategies; beneath each phrase, they require a thorough crossing of the ford. Phenomena and principle are not held as separate entities;
the partial and the perfect possess their respective hosts and guests. Wind and clouds now meet in this moment; with a single snap of the fingers, all is renewed.
Presented to Master Wuzhang:

The Flower Garland Pagoda at the front of the mountain, the Horse Stable and the Puguang Hall; outside the gate, the Ox Pen and the Field of Perfect Enlightenment. Fifty-three people were buried on the same day;
Sudhana ran until his feet grew sores.
The practitioner seeks a verse:
To whose hand has the creation been entrusted? You have come here to briefly relieve my countenance. If you wish to travel the celestial path, first break through the barrier of the ghost-gate.
Within the movements of fortune and misfortune, and within the square inch of the heart-mind, even a hair’s breadth of error results in transgressions as heavy as mountains.
The practitioner who seeks through verses finds that understanding the body is not as good as understanding the mind; when the mind is understood, the body has no cause for worry.
If both body and mind are fully understood, why should one seek further to be enfeoffed as an immortal or a marquis?
An Observer of the Path seeks a verse:
"The realms encountered since beginning one's study of the Buddha are many; if one cannot subdue them, they immediately become demons. To subdue demons, one must employ the dharma of non-mind;
then the six thieves will surrender their cities and all turn their spears."
Inscribed on the "Three Realms Diagram" by Teaching Master Zhongyi:
The clouds of the Great Purity are like dust within a mirror; from the root of non-abiding, they respond expansively like spring. Subtle and profound, they remain unmoving.
Manifesting boundlessly, universally entering the three periods of time—what is delusion and what is truth? This is a ready-made koan; why waste energy on it?
A single stroke at the head cuts off the vital pass.
A Small Assembly at Jingming Hermitage on Guanshan for Thirty-three Monks from Seventy States:
With donkey jaws and horse chins, you are loathed by all. If you masters elsewhere possessed hands capable of ensnaring them, Today they would have no cause to reach Jingming.

Inscription for the Small Pavilion at Yongning I have come once more to this land of Qingliang; The small chamber and its windows are exceptionally bright. It is not that the mountain folk monopolize the spring colors;
Rather, the nature of things naturally unfolds its own sentiments.
Presented to the Scholar Huishu, Two Poems:
In dealing with the world, let your eyes be as your brows; Naturally, the mind-ground will be free from fragmentation. Turning the body, you shall further penetrate the waves of the Dragon Gate;
Your horns and tusks so towering that the universe itself seems lowered.
The path before Shaoshi Cliff is not far; yet, as soon as one conceives of it, it stretches away. At evening on West Lake, I gaze upon the water;
a light breeze stirs the small boat as the painted oars dip down.
The Patriarch of Western Shu, Zhengdao, returned to his hometown seeking verses for the fifty-four military prefectures of Xichuan: "How many sons can nod their heads?
Having passed through the Jianmen Pass, they are elegant even in moments that are not ostentatious."

Spontaneous Verses on Staying Overnight at Jietian Staying overnight at the home of a lay practitioner (jushi) of Xishan, we sat around the hearth facing one another and spoke of our lives. From the very beginning, there has not been so much as a single thread of it;
it is simply the flowers before the eyes of a weary life.
Sent off, Supervisor Hong opens the sea-fields;
his lofty and dignified bearing seeks to take the lead. Seize the opportune moment early and apply the whip with vigor. Turn over the thousand acres of waves upon the riverbanks;
from this, the sacred sprouts shall flourish across the mulberry fields.
Seeing off Chan Master Xun as he returns to his hometown:
The gaze reaches the limit where clear waters reflect the void; White artemisia and red smartweed battle the western wind.
This profound meaning beyond three thousand miles— Who would dare with an iron bond burden the ancestors?
Two Verses Sent for Chan Practitioner Xiang You are one from the lineage of Ciming; you must transcend and excel to startle the multitude.
Only by leaping swiftly into the vast waves will the true pulse of Cao’an be seen to branch forth.
Parting at the head of the Turbid Harbor River, where azure clouds and autumn waters linger in gentle serenity. Do not disdain my old ineptitude and profound indolence;
I shall come again another day to knock upon your bamboo gate.
I thank my fellow practitioner Yang Shancai for the gift of this rosary.
Having set out on the journey southward, you did not lose your way; you have secured the vajra-bead behind the head. Holding it forth with both hands, you personally present it to me;
its brilliant radiance pierces the dark thoroughfare.
Hushi Miaoyuan requested this verse eight years ago while confined to her sickbed;
today she is at peace and well. In this peace and well-being, she constantly reflects upon the time of her suffering and illness.
Regarding the fundamental truth of suffering and joy, one must exert vigorous effort to sustain it.
Seeing Off Attendant Jie on His Return Home (The Lantern Festival of the Year Xinwei) A phrase of great penetration that strikes the vital point;
When facing him directly, the crown of the head is opened wide. We have followed one another for four years now; In our mutual inquiry and examination, there is not a trace left behind.
Though he has not yet been entrusted with the bowl and bag, his spirit and bearing swallow the heavens and earth. Yet he takes the Eye of the True Dharma and calls it a broken sand-pot.
On this journey to pay his respects, take care not to settle into a fixed root. I have a final instruction; wait until he returns, and I shall require you to follow this Buddhist service.

For this reason, when Chan Master Cigan entered his stupa, his *māheśvara* three eyes were thoroughly penetrating and impartial; that he fully upheld [the Dharma] at the end is precisely what is manifest here.
Thus, throughout his life, Chan Master Cigan carried his board alone, refusing all assignments. Having realized the oneness of self and others, he passed through birth and death.

The old nest and trap. Treading upon mountains of knives and trees of swords is like walking upon red lotuses; entering the cauldron of boiling water and the furnace of burning coals is like ascending a precious sanctuary.

One's entire being is this great gate of liberation; there is not even a single hair’s breadth of external object. Having finished his work of transforming conditions, he passes through by borrowing the way.
Within the samādhi of the blazing fire, he spontaneously incinerates his own body. The great flames reach to the heavens—who has eyes to behold them? Gold.

The sacred remains are brilliantly arrayed in five colors; their lofty traces are not obscured, radiating ever-fresh splendor. Today they are enshrined within the stūpa, severing the continuity of valley and mountain.
Ten thousand trees stir with wind; a thousand rivers reflect the moon. The true lamp and blazing flames increase the brilliance of Shaoshi.
At this very moment, how do you speak the phrase "shifting the body and changing the step"? Do you know where it lands?
A precious seal hangs in the void; its wondrous layers unfold like the opening of brocade seams. (He lets out a shout.)
For the purpose of the Retainer, the Grand Councilor, and the Grand Master of Ceremonies, the earth is vast and the heavens high;
the seas are wide and the mountains distant. He has manifested the supreme mechanism to reveal the true aspect.

Therefore, our Retainer, the Grand Councilor, has cleared the orthodox eye of the crown of his head and displayed the spiritual talisman behind his elbow; he does this for the sake of the state and the people.
By means of this ultimate loyalty and ultimate filiality, one may be said to perform great deeds without acting as their master; truly, such a person is seen to be a true adept.

At the final moment, they fully uphold the teaching, severing the ten directions of space. In the field of non-arising, there is sowing and harvesting; upon the vessel of Prajñā, there is the ferry and the crossing.
Having attained a state that transcends all things and walks alone upon the Great Path—at such a time as this, how do you express the single phrase of total reverence?
One must look beyond the clouds; a single sword leans against the heavens, cold.
Acting as the scribe for Nan, he brought down the fires at Donghu, Guanzhong, and Guizong.
Blazing with radiant brilliance within the furnace, his iron eyes and copper pupils could not be melted away;
the true core of the patch-robed monk is well worth circulating.
The Recorded Sayings of Master Ying’an, Volume Ten (End). Epitaph (Appendix),
composed by Li Hao, Court Gentleman of the Left,
Vice Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, concurrently acting as Acting Official of the Ministry of Personnel.
In the first year of the Longxing era, on the thirteenth day of the sixth month of the Guiwei year, Chan Master Tianhua Ying’an, the abbot of Mount Tiantong, passed away.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at the western foot of the monastery. His attendant, Xinghui, brought his final letter.
This is supplemented by the portrait of Zhaozhou. I requested a text to serve as an inscription. I replied, "I ought to compose this inscription.
In the year of Gengwu, I first met the Master in Fanyang; fourteen years have passed since then.

Whenever I felt a thought arise, even if it were a thousand li away, I would immediately dispatch a carriage to go to him, never remaining for even a brief moment. This has been my constant practice, whether at home or in office.
He resided there, and his disciples came and went for the sake of his teachings without ever ceasing.
Knowing the details of the Master’s travels with great clarity, it is fitting that I compose this inscription to demonstrate the faith of those who enter and to guide them toward further progress.

After a long time, the fundamental Dharma will manifest itself in its full brilliance, leaving no room for evasion. Upon examining its ultimate limit, it is identical to what our Confucian tradition calls "the single thread" (yiguan).

The two extremes—the beauty of the ancestral temple and the abundance of the hundred officials—none can surpass it; the sun and moon cannot be climbed to its heights, and Heaven never fails it by even a fraction.
I know that what my Master has created is exhaustive and complete. It is fitting that I compose this inscription. To refuse would be a failure in my duty as his disciple.
Furthermore, he has entrusted me with the likeness of an ancient Buddha to convey his intent; it is my responsibility to inscribe it. How could I decline? My Master was of the Jiang clan.
Zi was a native of Huangmei. From birth he was extraordinary and outstanding; his physical frame and features were lofty and refined.

Even in his childhood, he grew weary of the world and thus possessed a resolute will to ferry across all beings. At the age of seventeen, he left the household life at Dongchan Monastery in his home district. The following year, he became a full monk (*bhikṣu*).
The year after that, he took up his staff and traveled to visit teachers, first calling upon Master Suishui of Suizhou to receive his tonsure.
Tasting the flavor of the Dharma, he was filled with joy and exultation. He subsequently traveled throughout the regions of north and south Hunan, as well as east and west Jiangxi.

Wherever he went, he engaged in vigorous debate with various senior masters, finding perfect accord with them all. Nevertheless, the Master’s spiritual capacity was vast and profound; he refused to be satisfied with a mere modicum of attainment.
He requested instruction from Shangqian Zhui, who had thoroughly penetrated the ultimate depths. Though surrounded by all the Buddhas and patriarchs, he did not dwell upon a single point.
Having fulfilled his initial vow, he then went up to Yunju to pay respects to Chan Master Yuanwu. Upon their first meeting, Yuanwu patted him in encouragement and sternly exhorted him.
For the sake of the Dharma, he performed arduous labors and ran about, fearing only that he might fall behind. Eventually, Yuanwu...
He entered Shu and was directed to go see Changjiao Long; Yu Xuan was Long’s son. When Long moved to Huqiu, the Master truly acted as his vanguard.
Within less than half a year, he had thoroughly mastered the Great Dharma and suddenly clarified the essential point of Yuanwu’s personhood.

His spiritual mechanisms were profound and firm, and his applications were vast and expansive; the utterances that issued from him all transcended conventional standards and surpassed ordinary measure, such that neither humans nor devas could fathom them.
His reputation for the Way spread widely throughout the monastic communities. Before long, he took his leave and traveled freely among various regions.
Initially, while serving as a co-preacher at Lianyun in Chuzhou, Chu-shou invited him to assume the abbacy under the name Miaoyan; subsequently, he resided at Mingguo in Quzhou.
Qi’s Dezhang; Raoyang’s Baoen and Jianfu; Wuzhou’s Baolin and Baoen; Jiangxi’s Donglin and Jiankang’s Jiangshan;

Pingjiang’s Wanshou; twice residing at Nankang’s Guizong; and finally residing at today’s Tiantong—everywhere he was revered by both monastics and laypeople, who unanimously petitioned for his appointment.
In each location, he opened the great gate of giving and extended his hand to save others.

Upon his awakening, people from near and far flocked to him like water rushing into a valley. Whether in general discourses (*pūsè*), small-scale sermons (*xiǎocān*), or in the context of questions, answers, and cross-examinations, the Master was always composed and leisurely, exhausting every skillful means (*upāya*).
His dynamic discernment within the meditation hall—alternating between restraint and release, killing and giving life—was particularly renowned for its brilliance and subtlety.

Even those who had long studied under other masters and were thoroughly versed in the teachings would break into a cold sweat and feel their spirits die away the moment they approached the Master’s mallet and whisk; they lamented that they had met him too late.
He anticipated our needs and exerted his efforts, accomplishing what was difficult to assemble in order to report his services.

Those who had previously led disciples and presided over monasteries all concealed their names and traces, considering it a blessing merely to have their robes and bowls placed among the lower ranks. Alas! How vast is the Way!

Having greatly revitalized the tradition of his school and serving as an eye for the world, the Master’s conduct and integrity were so lofty and pure that they are entirely worthy of praise and recounting.
When the Master first attained enlightenment, he traveled together with Chan Master Cigan—who was then known as Yuan Budai—to engage in mutual inquiry and refinement.
Their practice grew increasingly profound day by day. Later, when they reached Huguo Temple, they found great joy in each other’s company. Cigan—
Regarding his intention to depart, although he was not without a sense of belonging toward his teacher, once he had opened the hall and succeeded to the Dharma, he never forgot Huqiu.
This is quite different from those of recent times who are dazzled by fame and entangled by gain, burning incense without tracing its source.
His standards were strict and severe; if anyone committed a transgression, he would often confront them face-to-face, allowing no leniency. Once the words were out of his mouth, they were final.
He was liberated and without interval. Because of this, students feared and looked up to him. Whenever he presided over a monastery, he responded universally and received with detachment;
yet, even when managing minor matters or small details, he always acted with infinite foresight and never behaved with negligence.
If even the slightest thing did not accord with his mind, he would simply depart abruptly, unable to be turned back or dissuaded. He once said of himself: "For those of us who are monks..."

Wearing straw sandals, he resided in the monastery as if a viper were loath to leave its den. He exhorted his disciples with diligence, forbidding them from being lax, and he invariably led by personal example in every matter.
Even when he was about to manifest illness, he would still hang his name plaque and enter the room; this continued until the late hours of the night for many days.
When it became clear he was nearing the end, someone requested that he recite a verse on departing this world. The Master said, "I have often laughed at those of other quarters."
Did he act for others, or did he act for himself? He attended to the affairs of the monastery with such meticulous care that not even the smallest detail was neglected.
Suddenly, he sat cross-legged and passed away. He was sixty-one years of age and forty-three years since his ordination. His verses and recorded sayings were extremely numerous;

though they had not yet been formally edited and arranged, they were already widely circulated throughout the world. As for Chan Master Miaoxi of Mount Jing, his reputation was most eminent. Just as he was becoming prominent—
At that time, amidst the intense pressure of those who sought to humble him, the Master maintained his customary decorum without adding or subtracting anything.

Later, while he was at Mei Yang, a monk brought a record of the Master’s *chuishu* (profound instructions). When Miaoxi saw it, he praised it with the utmost fervor. He subsequently sent a verse back to Guizong, which said:
"Severing all paths atop the First Peak of the Golden Wheel, A thousand demons and a hundred monsters have all hidden their traces. In recent years, I have further attained the True [Dharma]..."
The *Xiaoxi* reports that the true lineage of Yangqi has been transmitted; such is the emphasis placed upon it.

When Miaoxi returned to Mount Jing and retired to the Moonlight Hermitage (*Mingyue-an*), the Master propagated the teachings in Mingzhou. As these uncle and nephew were situated across from one another, travelers coming and going in great numbers invariably visited the gates of these two Great Beings.
All said without dissent: "Miaoxi and Yan'an are no different. This was before even a month had passed since the Master’s passing.
When Miaoxi also passes away through transformation, will the ancestral Way not eventually decline? The later generations are to be feared;
there will surely be those who succeed him. The inscription says:
The single school of Linji branched out into various lineages; it flourished through Yangqi and reached its peak under Wuzu, who possessed both excellence and beauty.
It was indeed Yuanwu who produced sons and grandsons, further strengthening the gate.
This master appeared later, his spirit dominating all quarters; having initiated the tradition at Shuinan, he traveled extensively throughout the lakes and rivers to seek instruction.

Wherever he went, all were subdued; his array was magnificent and grand. Yet when the army looked on, it seemed empty; soaring high and galloping afar, he reached the very summit and depths of the Dharma.
By means of ladders and rafts—mallets, brushes, cloths, and water bottles—he manifested unconditioned compassion across thirteen monasteries.
Uttering fearless teachings, though there were tens of thousands of demonic hordes, he could both slay them and bring them to life.
Driving away the plow and seizing from the hungry; With the wisdom of stillness and movement, one extracts [the essence].
Returning to that which is primordial, One attains this great penetration. Before the Taibai Peak, Beneath the Linglong Rock, There is a stūpa, In which the sacred relics reside.
The talk of thirty years hence Is still like closing one's eyes in the night.

The Memorial for Vice Minister Li (Appendix) On the thirteenth day of the sixth month of the first year of Longxing, Li Hao— holding the rank of Left Assistant in the Imperial Council, serving as Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
and concurrently acting as Official of the Ministry of Personnel— respectfully presents this offering of incense and tea to perform a sacrifice at [the grave of]...
Therefore, the Venerable Master Ying’an of Mount Tiandong—alas! The Master has finally passed into stillness.
Now, it is said that if one does not offer sacrifices, they will not come; yet when sacrifices are offered, they truly arrive.
Just as he was wandering south of the waters, moving to and fro between the east and west of the Yangtze and the north and south of the Lake, and struggling amidst Yunju and Zhangjiao.
For such a long time, he was like one searching for a lost son, or as if mourning the death of his parents; this was because he had not yet awakened.
Yet, even then, he was surely majestic and dignified, brilliant and resplendent.

Subsequently, he alone occupied the Dharma-seat for fifteen years, preaching the Dharma like thunder and wind, driving monks about like phoenixes and qilin; this was because he had already awakened. Furthermore—
There has never been a time when one was not limping and dragging along, a hundred deformities and a thousand clumsinesses. To forge and smelt all Buddhas—this is indeed a state of no-merit;
yet it is also the most supreme merit. To scold and rebuke all Patriarchs—this is indeed a state of no-virtue;
yet it is also the peerless virtue. When I ran to my teacher, we looked at each other and laughed; giver and receiver were both forgotten. Thus it was in the past.

For those who are beginners, I do not now rely on past habituation. That the Huai and Yangtze rivers flow from different sources does not constitute an obstacle; that Confucianism and Buddhism have different outward forms does not constitute a separation.

To follow me daily with staff and sandals, gazing upon my mallet and whisk, does not constitute intimacy; to let years and cycles pass without understanding even a single character or phrase does not constitute distance.
To inquire and consult while alive does not constitute reverence; to refrain from weeping or attending a funeral when one dies does not constitute disrespect. This is goodness.
Observing those who followed the Master, at a single offering, they perceived him as having no further residual aggregates (*skandha*); may he enjoy [this merit].

Prefaced by an introduction from the Senior Minister, Grand Councilor, and State Counselor, Mr. Qian; and with funds provided by the Grand Tutor, Prince of Heyi, Mr. Yang, these were carved onto printing blocks.
Both of them served as ramparts for the Gate of the Dharma, acting as patrons of the teachings; their capacity was like that of the vast ocean, overflowing its bounds.

The ocean of Prajñā enables those who see and hear it to obtain benefit; through it, delusion and awakening transcend the realm of emotion. A single thought encompasses empty space, and the three periods of time are entirely equal.
Truly, these words apply to the Great Layman who became a Buddha and a Patriarch.
Written with reverence on an auspicious day in the first month of the Bingxu year of the Qian Dao era by the mountain-dwelling bhikṣu Shouchuan.

In the *Pǔshuō* (General Discourse) of Master Sōngyuán, it is said that when the ancestral teacher Yìng’ān was first traveling as a wandering monk (*xiézhú*), he resided under a certain venerable elder (*zūnxǔ*).

"One cannot pass it. Again, "Passing it in such a way, one still cannot pass it. The two men deliberated thus until they were unconsciously awakened by the crowing of a cock;

The Dharma practice of Master Suinan Sui of Suizhou was that of a venerable patriarch of the Dongshan lineage.

When the official En went directly to visit him, he paid his respects and immediately returned to the hall. There was a brother monk there who shared a single mat with him; he sat in meditation for long periods and did not associate with others.
One day, the Master asked him, "Do you sleep little? The monk replied in a stern voice, "Elder brother, nowadays..."
"What kind of season is this? Do you still have time to sleep? At these words, the Master’s face flushed with heat and sweat poured down.

He immediately resolved his will and, without ceasing day or night, took awakening as his standard. In less than a month, he experienced an initial breakthrough while sitting alone on his meditation platform.
The Master’s Patriarch (Shizu) had also provided an elucidation. From then on, whenever [Zhaozhou] entered the room, he would seize the path and carry it away;
consequently, the Master was unable to deal with him. One day, while entering the room, [the Master] called out, "Brother Hua, you are quite good, yet you have not yet clarified the public case.
Shizu raised his voice and said, "The entire great earth is a single public case. How can you, Master, [deal with this]?"
Shengming bowed his head, whereupon the Master said, "This old fellow has not yet understood me. He packed his belongings and headed for the abbot’s quarters;
after prostrating three times, he departed. Hearing that Yuanwu was residing at Yunju, he went directly to the monastery.
Whenever they met for private instruction, their minds accorded with one another on every occasion for several sessions. However, Yuanwu never brought up the ultimate core of the teaching.
He was able to open his mouth [to speak]. Yuanwu often said to others, "This man from Qizhou has attained it, but he simply lacks that one final blow to the back of the head.
When Yuanwu returned to Shu, the Master (Zhaozhou) wished to follow him there as well. Yuanwu said, "You need not follow me;
there are Head Seat Dahui, Attendant Yuan, and Librarian Long of Zhangjiao, whose insights are equal to my own."

"I am just like the old monk. Go and see him; he will surely settle the Great Matter for you. Thereupon, following these instructions, he went specifically to Changjiao in Xuanzhou to visit Master Long.
The master’s gate was solitary and steep, such that there was no room for anyone to settle there. Before many months had passed, Long moved to Huqiu, and [the student] followed him there as well.
Subsequently, he was requested to serve as the *karmadāna* (Rector). One day, in the meditation hall, [Long] raised the Five...
When the Patriarch was leading his ox past the window and engaged in conversation, as [Zhaozhou] was about to offer a response, the Patriarch struck him a blow across the chest with his fist.
From that moment, Zhaozhou’s life-root (mìnggēn) was severed. At that time, Master Long wished to appoint him as the head of the assembly.

An elder named Yuanwu in the congregation remarked, "Huairang is still too tender. When the Master Patriarch heard this, he inscribed a verse upon the wall, saying: "The green mountains by the river are truly..."
"Not yet old; let the spring colors at the head of the house unfold slowly. People say the peach blossoms in the cave are tender;
perhaps there is no such branch in the human world. Without further ado, he departed. This was Master Yuan of Ciana, who at that time resided at Lianyun in Chu-zhou.
My late master said, "When I was formerly at Yunju, I always found this fellow tasteless. Looking back now, it may not necessarily be so."
"He has reached my fields; let me go and see for myself what he is up to. As soon as he arrived, he went straight to the abbot’s quarters.
The attendant announced his arrival. Hearing this, Chan Master Huanzhu hurried out. Upon seeing him, he said, "Brother Hua, congratulations on this occasion;
it seems your great matter is now finally settled. The Master said, "Before I had even opened my mouth, he already knew. Truly, one must have attained this realization.
When people meet, they do not rely on forms or words; they immediately know where one has landed. This is the very model for practicing Chan.
How could it be like the way masters and students nowadays meet, exchanging line by line, until at the end one adds an extra phrase and considers that a victory in Chan?
In the end, they do not know its depth or shallowness, because they have never truly trodden the path.
"Adhering to the True Lineage (Zhengmai) means making one's livelihood solely within words and phrases... (and so forth).
